title: Gandhi's Indigo Truth
subtitle: How a village notebook shook an empire
moral: Truth grows powerful when it is patiently recorded.

sources.citation: M.K. Gandhi, An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, Champaran chapters
sources.note: Participant account of the inquiry, arrest and settlement.

sources.citation: Government of Bihar and Orissa, Report of the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee (1917)
sources.note: Official record acknowledging planter abuses and recommending reform.

sources.citation: Jacques Pouchepadass, Champaran and Gandhi: Planters, Peasants and Gandhian Politics (1999)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction using planter and district records.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Gandhi standing amid indigo fields under a harsh sun

dialogue.text: Champaran, 1917: a quiet lawyer with a notebook walked into the indigo fields—and forced the Raj to record its own injustice.

panels.shot: intimate mid-shot inside a Calcutta gathering, slightly low angle on Gandhi

dialogue.text: Before Champaran, Gandhi was still a newcomer in Indian politics, better known for South Africa than for any village in Bihar.

panels.shot: tight close-up on Gandhi’s hands as a determined peasant grips them

dialogue.text: There, a persistent indigo cultivator, Raj Kumar Shukla, seized his hand and refused to let go until he promised to see Champaran.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of Gandhi looking out from a train compartment

dialogue.speaker: mahatma_gandhi
dialogue.text: I must see with my own eyes before I speak.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of a Champaran village, slightly elevated

dialogue.text: Champaran was not a battlefield, but a quiet countryside locked in a harsh contract called tinkathia—three kathas of every bigha forced under indigo.

panels.shot: mid-shot inside a poor peasant hut, candlelit, Gandhi seated on the floor

dialogue.text: Tenant after tenant spoke of leases they could not read, of forced indigo, of low returns and heavy illegal exactions when they tried to escape.

panels.shot: close-up on Gandhi’s notebook and face, lit by a small lamp

dialogue.text: Gandhi did not call for revolt. He opened a notebook. He wrote names, rents, beatings, dates—turning whispered misery into a record.

panels.shot: formal mid-shot in a colonial office, slight low angle on a magistrate facing Gandhi

dialogue.text: The district authorities ordered him to leave Champaran. Gandhi read the order, reflected, and quietly wrote his reply.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Gandhi standing outside the court, surrounded by peasants and lawyers

dialogue.speaker: mahatma_gandhi
dialogue.text: I obey the law of conscience. I will not leave Champaran.

panels.shot: wide shot inside the courtroom packed with peasants, lawyers in front rows

dialogue.text: The magistrate, faced with a nonviolent refusal and an unexpected crowd, postponed sentence. Gandhi’s quiet defiance forced the government to rethink its own order.

panels.shot: group mid-shot of Gandhi with Indian lawyers in a verandah meeting

dialogue.text: He turned to the lawyers of Bihar, asking them not just to argue in court, but to live among the peasants and share the risk of disobeying.

panels.shot: dynamic montage-like wide shot of multiple huts with Gandhi’s team taking statements

dialogue.text: Over weeks, they gathered hundreds of statements. Each was a story of rent, coercion, beatings; together they became evidence no file could ignore.

panels.shot: interior shot of a planter’s bungalow verandah, planter and Gandhi seated opposite

dialogue.text: He also met the planters, neither flattering nor provoking, asking them to explain tinkathia and their claims, and quietly comparing their words with the villagers’ accounts.

panels.shot: mid-shot of Gandhi writing a letter at a simple desk, lantern beside him

dialogue.text: By now, the government knew he had not stirred a riot, but an inquiry. The Lieutenant-Governor’s council decided to appoint an official committee.

panels.shot: formal group wide shot of the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee in session

dialogue.text: In 1917, the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee began its work. Gandhi, now inside the machinery of the Raj, laid out the peasants’ testimony as disciplined fact.

panels.shot: close-up of Gandhi speaking calmly in the committee, others listening

dialogue.speaker: mahatma_gandhi
dialogue.text: We do not ask for favour. We ask that what is written be believed.

panels.shot: medium shot of a British official reading aloud from the committee report draft

dialogue.text: The official report acknowledged planter abuses and recommended partial refund of illegal exactions, and the gradual ending of the tinkathia system.

panels.shot: wide shot of a village gathering as a volunteer explains the settlement to peasants

dialogue.text: This was no instant miracle. Planters resisted, and withdrawal from indigo took time. Yet for the first time, the system itself had been condemned by the state’s own pen.

panels.shot: intimate mid-shot of Gandhi starting a village school with children around

dialogue.text: Even as reforms moved slowly, Gandhi stayed to start schools, clean villages and build habits of self-respect that would outlast any one settlement.

panels.shot: quiet close-up of Gandhi closing his notebook, soft light on his face

dialogue.text: Champaran became Gandhi’s first great satyagraha in India—a struggle not of slogans but of patient documentation, disciplined refusal and negotiated reform.

panels.shot: epic high wide shot of the Champaran landscape with distant peasants at work

dialogue.text: In Champaran, truth did not shout; it was written, signed and read into the record—and in that quiet act, a village’s suffering began to bend an empire’s law.
